passage: Lakshmi waited forty minutes at Ernakulam station in the rain, phone dead, before taking an auto home. Jomon had forgotten. Again. On the ride, her mind started its old swing: he doesn't care, he never did. Then she stopped herself and did what she had been practising. She said quietly, under her breath, "Jomon is caring. Jomon is also careless." She made herself list both. Caring: he had sat up with her through her father's surgery; he remembered her mother's medicines. Careless: the station, twice now. Both were real. When she got home and he rushed to the door, apologising, she didn't explode or pretend it was fine. "I'm hurt," she said. "And I know you love me. Can we set up a reminder system?"

qa.q: How long did Lakshmi wait at the station?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: What swing did Lakshmi's mind start on the auto ride?
qa.a: A hurt, angry swing toward "he doesn't care, he never did".

qa.q: What did Lakshmi do to hold both truths?
qa.a: She said aloud that Jomon is caring and also careless, listed examples of both, then told him she was hurt while asking for a reminder system.

qa.q: How might Jomon feel at the door?
qa.a: Guilty and anxious, rushing to apologise, and relieved that she didn't explode.

grounding: An adult reminds herself a person can be both caring and careless, and responds steadily instead of swinging to all bad.

passage:
"Papa missed my graduation, Nitin. He said he'd be there."
"I know. He mixed up the date."
"Last week I'd have said he's the best father in the world. Today I want to say he's the worst."
"Which one is true?"
Kashish sighed. "Neither. Both? He drove me to every exam for three years. He also forgets things that matter to me."
"That sounds like Papa."
"I'm trying to hold both. Caring and careless. It's harder than picking one."
"Picking one is easier for about a day."
"Then it explodes."
"Exactly. So what will you tell him?"
"That I'm hurt. And that I know he loves me. Both."

qa.q: What did Papa do for three years?
qa.a: Drove Kashish to every exam.

qa.q: What does Kashish feel today about Papa?
qa.a: Hurt and angry enough to want to call him the worst father, while knowing that isn't the whole truth.

qa.q: What does Kashish plan to tell Papa?
qa.a: That Kashish is hurt, and knows he loves them: both truths together.

qa.q: How does Nitin help?
qa.a: Nitin asks which one is true and agrees that picking one explodes later, helping Kashish hold both.

grounding: An adult holds that a father is both caring and careless, and plans to say both instead of swinging to one.

passage: For years, my friendship with Nikita swung like a pendulum. When she remembered my birthday with a handmade card, she was my soulmate. When she cancelled on me twice in a month, she was selfish and I'd think about ending it. Last year a friend asked me, "Is she good or bad?" and I realised the question itself was the problem. Nikita is generous, and she is disorganised. She's loyal, and she forgets plans. Both are simply true. Now, when she cancels, I say, "That's annoying, and I still love you." I also book our plans for weekends, when she's less stretched. I'm Vinita, and our friendship is calmer than it has ever been.

qa.q: What did Nikita make for Vinita's birthday?
qa.a: A handmade card.

qa.q: How did Vinita use to feel when Nikita cancelled?
qa.a: Hurt and angry enough to think Nikita was selfish and to consider ending the friendship.

qa.q: What does Vinita do now?
qa.a: Holds both truths, says "That's annoying, and I still love you", and books plans for weekends when Nikita is less stretched.

qa.q: How might Nikita experience the calmer friendship?
qa.a: More relaxed and secure, no longer swinging between soulmate and selfish in Vinita's eyes.

grounding: An adult learns to see a friend as both generous and disorganised, which makes the friendship steadier.

passage:
Monday, a cold winter morning: Jasleen shuffles around the flat in Papa's big slippers, flap, flap. "I'm going to the hospital," she says, in his deep voice.
Wednesday: She lines up her dolls and listens to their tummies with a toy stethoscope. "Breathe in. Good girl. Drink warm water," she says, exactly like Papa.
Saturday: Her little cousin Kalyani wants a turn. Jasleen hands her the stethoscope and puts Papa's reading glasses on her own nose. "Now I'm the big doctor," she says, standing very tall. Papa, watching from the door, grins and hands her his old white coat.

qa.q: What did Jasleen listen to the dolls' tummies with?
qa.a: A toy stethoscope.

qa.q: How does Jasleen feel wearing Papa's glasses?
qa.a: Proud, big and grown-up, standing very tall like the doctor Papa she admires.

qa.q: How does Papa respond, and why does it help?
qa.a: He grins and gives her his old white coat, encouraging her play instead of teasing, so she feels big and safe.

qa.q: How might Kalyani feel getting the stethoscope?
qa.a: Excited and included, getting to join the game.

grounding: A preschooler wears her father's slippers and copies his doctor phrases, feeling big and safe like him.

passage: The power went out on a sticky summer afternoon, and the fan stopped. The grown-ups groaned. But Gurleen wrapped Mummy's dupatta round her shoulders, stepped into Mummy's school sandals, and clapped her hands. "Class, sit down! No talking!" she said, exactly the way Mummy said it at the school where she taught. Her little brother Imran sat on the floor. Gurleen drew on the wall chalkboard, wobbling in the big sandals. "Very good, Imran. Gold star!" Mummy, fanning herself, laughed. "Who taught you that?" "You did," Gurleen said, standing tall. "I'm the teacher now."

qa.q: What did Gurleen wrap round her shoulders?
qa.a: Mummy's dupatta.

qa.q: How does Gurleen feel being the teacher?
qa.a: Proud and big, standing tall and feeling in charge, like Mummy.

qa.q: How could Mummy support this play?
qa.a: Laugh warmly, as she does, and join in, letting Gurleen try on the role she admires.

qa.q: How might Imran feel as the student?
qa.a: Happy to play along, especially when he gets a gold star.

grounding: A preschooler dresses in her mother's dupatta and sandals and copies her teacher phrases, feeling big and safe.

passage: On Holi morning in their Jaipur flat, Nitin clomped around in Papa's big black shoes, laces trailing. "Minakshi, have you finished your homework?" he asked his sister, frowning like Papa. Minakshi burst out laughing. Then he picked up Papa's phone, held it to his ear, and said, "Yes, yes, send the file by five." Papa, coming in with the colours, stopped. "Is that me?" Nitin nodded, very serious. "I'm the papa today." Papa squatted down, took off his cap and put it on Nitin's head. "Then the papa gets to throw the first colour." Nitin beamed and marched out, shoes flapping.

qa.q: What did Nitin say on the pretend phone call?
qa.a: "Yes, yes, send the file by five."

qa.q: How does Nitin feel being the papa?
qa.a: Serious, proud and big, trying on the power of the adult he admires.

qa.q: What did Papa's response give Nitin?
qa.a: Delight and a sense of being taken seriously: Papa gave him the cap and let him throw the first colour.

qa.q: How does Minakshi react?
qa.a: She bursts out laughing, amused at her little brother playing Papa.

grounding: A preschooler clomps around in his father's shoes and copies his phrases, feeling big and safe like him.

passage: Manoj, you've cut your hair like that fast bowler on TV, haven't you? When I was ten, your Swati nani did the same. There was a famous batswoman then, and I copied everything: her short hair, the way she tapped her bat twice, even her walk. That summer I felt brave, as if some of her strength had got into me. I practised every evening because she did. But I also copied her glare at bowlers, and one day I shouted at a younger girl who dropped a catch, the way I'd seen my hero do. My coach took me aside: "Copy her practice, Swati. Not her temper." I cried, but I remembered it. You can keep the haircut, beta. Just choose what else you borrow.

qa.q: How many times did the batswoman tap her bat?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: How did young Swati feel copying her hero?
qa.a: Brave and strong, as if some of the hero's strength had got into her.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: Her coach telling her to copy the hero's practice, not her temper, after she shouted at a younger girl.

qa.q: How might the younger girl who dropped the catch have felt?
qa.a: Hurt and scared, shouted at by an older player for one mistake.

grounding: An elder recalls copying a sporting hero as a child, gaining courage but also importing a harsh attitude.

passage: All through the monsoon, the colony cricket matches kept getting rained off, but Yogesh practised his hero's stance in the corridor anyway: bat high, collar up, chin raised. He had even asked the barber for the same spiky hair as the famous opener on TV. When he batted, he felt taller. At the one match that finally happened, he hit two fours and then stared the bowler down, just like on TV, and said, "Is that all you've got?" The bowler, a small boy from B-block, looked like he might cry. Yogesh's sister Hansa marched onto the field. "Your hero practises for hours. Copy that. Not the staring." Yogesh's ears went red. He mumbled sorry to the bowler.

qa.q: How many fours did Yogesh hit?
qa.a: Two.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel batting in his hero's style?
qa.a: Taller and more confident, as if he shared some of the hero's strength.

qa.q: What was Hansa's advice?
qa.a: To copy the hero's hours of practice, not the staring and the swagger.

qa.q: How might the small bowler have felt?
qa.a: Upset and small, close to tears after being taunted.

grounding: A boy copies a cricketer's stance, hair and swagger, and learns to keep the practice but drop the taunting.

passage: In the Christmas holidays, Deepika watched every match of the women's cricket tournament on TV in their Bengaluru flat. By New Year she had the same ponytail as her favourite captain, the same wristband, and the same way of pointing at the sky after a good shot. At the park she practised the captain's calm walk out to bat. "You even talk like her now," her friend Noor laughed. It was true. When Deepika missed a catch, she didn't cry like before; she clapped once and said, "Next ball," just like her hero. But when she hit a six, she also shouted "Too easy!" at Noor, who was bowling. Noor frowned. Deepika paused, then grinned sheepishly. "Okay, she doesn't say that part."

qa.q: What did Deepika do after a good shot?
qa.a: Pointed at the sky.

qa.q: How did Deepika feel now when she missed a catch?
qa.a: Steadier and calmer; instead of crying, she clapped once, feeling some of her hero's composure.

qa.q: What did Deepika's admiration teach her, and what went too far?
qa.a: Calm resilience, "Next ball"; the "Too easy!" taunt went too far, and she noticed it herself.

qa.q: How did Noor react to "Too easy!"?
qa.a: Noor frowned, a bit hurt or annoyed as the bowler.

grounding: A girl copies her cricket hero's style and calm, but catches herself importing a boastful taunt.

passage: Jeevan, I need to tell you something I'm not proud of. You know how the seniors used to call me names in Class 8 and push my bag off the bench? I hated it. I felt tiny. This year there's a new boy, small, with a stammer. And last week I found myself copying his stammer in the corridor, and everyone laughed. For one second I felt safe. Like I was on the other side now. Then I saw his face. It was my face from Class 8. I'm Pema, and I became the thing I hated. After school that same day I went to Ms Rai and told her everything, and she called the boy's parents and mine. Tomorrow I'm apologising to him, with her there.

qa.q: What did Pema copy in the corridor?
qa.a: The new boy's stammer.

qa.q: Why did copying the stammer feel safe for a moment?
qa.a: Pema had felt tiny and powerless when bullied, and taking the powerful role felt safer than being the victim.

qa.q: What did Pema do next, and why is it right?
qa.a: Told Ms Rai everything that same day; she called both families, and Pema will apologise with her present, which stops the harm.

qa.q: How might the new boy have felt?
qa.a: Humiliated and hurt, just as Pema once felt, especially with everyone laughing.

grounding: A teenager who was bullied starts mocking a weaker student, feels the pull of power, then stops and tells a teacher the same day.

passage:
Monday: Damini, who spent last year being called "hippo" by the girls in her old section, hears Keerthana, the new girl, mispronounce a word in English class. At lunch Damini imitates her. The girls around her laugh, and Damini feels, for the first time in a year, on the winning side.
Wednesday: Damini does it again, louder. Keerthana eats alone by the water tank.
Friday: Keerthana's eyes are red in first period. The class teacher, Mrs Pillai, keeps Damini back at lunch and asks calmly what has been happening. Damini starts to deny it, then cries. "They did it to me last year." Mrs Pillai listens, then says, "I know. And now Keerthana feels what you felt." That afternoon she calls both families and brings the two girls together to talk.

qa.q: What was Damini called last year?
qa.a: "Hippo."

qa.q: How did Damini feel when the girls laughed at her imitation?
qa.a: For the first time in a year she felt on the winning side, safer and more powerful.

qa.q: How did Mrs Pillai respond?
qa.a: She kept Damini back calmly, listened, said Keerthana now feels what Damini felt, called both families that afternoon and brought the girls together.

qa.q: What was it like for Keerthana that week?
qa.a: Isolating and painful; she ate alone by the water tank and came in with red eyes.

grounding: A teenager who was bullied begins mocking a new girl, repeating the harm, until a teacher steps in the day she notices.

passage: Suraj, you said the boys who teased you now tease someone else, and you've joined in? Let me tell you about your Hemant chacha at fifteen. In the hostel, the seniors made me polish their shoes and called me "chuha". When I became a senior, I did the same to a thin boy from Bihar. It felt good, I'm ashamed to say. Like I had finally climbed out of the pit. One night the warden caught me, and instead of shouting, he asked, "Hemant, who made you polish shoes?" I couldn't answer. That same night he told my father, and the next morning he made me apologise to the boy. I never did it again. You don't climb out of the pit by pushing someone else into it, beta.

qa.q: What did the seniors call young Hemant?
qa.a: "Chuha."

qa.q: Why did bullying the younger boy feel good to young Hemant?
qa.a: After being humiliated, taking the powerful role felt like climbing out of the pit; he felt safer, though he is ashamed of it now.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: The warden catching him and asking who made him polish shoes, telling his father that night, and making him apologise the next morning.

qa.q: How might the thin boy from Bihar have felt?
qa.a: Humiliated and trapped, just as Hemant once felt.

grounding: An elder recalls becoming a bully after being bullied, and how a warden's question stopped the cycle.

subtype: Absorbing a mentor's way of speaking [Actor]
passage: Abhinav, you'll laugh, but when I joined the newsroom as a trainee, I copied everything about my senior, Rao sir. His "Right, let's crack on." His habit of tapping his pen twice before an interview. Even the way he leaned back in his chair. Honestly, it made me braver. When I said "Right, let's crack on," I felt like I knew what I was doing. But a few months in, I interviewed a nervous farmer, and Rao sir's brisk style made the man clam up. That's when I realised I had to test what actually fit me. I'm Wasim, and I'm softer than Rao sir. I kept the pen tap. I dropped the leaning back. Now my interviews sound like me.

qa.q: What did Rao sir say before starting?
qa.a: "Right, let's crack on."

qa.q: How did copying Rao sir make Wasim feel?
qa.a: Braver and more confident, as if Wasim knew what to do.

qa.q: How did Wasim turn imitation into a personal style?
qa.a: After the brisk style failed with the nervous farmer, Wasim tested each habit, kept the pen tap and dropped the leaning back.

qa.q: How might the nervous farmer have experienced the brisk style?
qa.a: Rushed and uncomfortable, so he clammed up.

grounding: A trainee absorbs a senior's phrases and feels confident, then tests which habits genuinely fit.

subtype: Absorbing a mentor's way of speaking [Actor]
passage:
Week one: Vandana, a trainee at an architecture firm, notices how her senior, Devika, opens every client meeting: "Let's walk through your day in this house." Vandana writes it down.
Week five: Vandana uses the same line with her first small client, and the same way of sketching while talking. She feels calm and capable, as if Devika has lent her some confidence.
Week twelve: A family whose son uses a wheelchair needs something different. Devika's line doesn't fit; the parents want to talk about their worries, not a daily routine. Vandana hesitates, then asks her own question: "What worries you most about moving?" The meeting goes beautifully. Afterwards she keeps Devika's sketching habit, but writes her own opening line in her notebook.

qa.q: What was Devika's opening line?
qa.a: "Let's walk through your day in this house."

qa.q: How did Vandana feel using Devika's line in week five?
qa.a: Calm and capable, as if Devika had lent her some confidence.

qa.q: How did Vandana move from imitation to her own style?
qa.a: When the borrowed line didn't fit, she asked her own question, then kept the sketching habit and wrote her own opening.

qa.q: How might the family in week twelve have felt?
qa.a: Heard and reassured, since Vandana asked about their worries.

grounding: A trainee borrows her senior's phrases and feels confident, then tests what fits and finds her own style.

subtype: Absorbing a mentor's way of speaking [Actor]
passage: Mridul, you've started saying "basically" at the end of every sentence, just like your boss. Let me tell you about your Mehak bua at twenty. I was a trainee teacher, and I copied everything my senior did: her "Eyes on me, little ones", the way she clapped twice, even her strict eyebrow. It helped, beta. With her words in my mouth I felt like a real teacher. But one day a shy girl froze when I did the strict eyebrow. My senior could do it with warmth; on me it looked cold. So I watched myself for a month. I kept the clap and the "eyes on me". I dropped the eyebrow and added a silly song of my own. Borrow first, then keep only what fits you.

qa.q: How many times did the senior clap?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: How did young Mehak feel using her senior's words?
qa.a: Like a real teacher, more confident and capable.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Mehak's story?
qa.a: A shy girl freezing at the strict eyebrow, which led Mehak to watch herself, keep what fit and drop the rest.

qa.q: How might the shy girl have felt?
qa.a: Frightened by the cold look, freezing in place.

grounding: An elder recalls copying a senior's phrases as a trainee, then testing which fit and building her own style.

subtype: Choosing which parental traits to keep [Response]
passage: Supervisor's note, Thursday. Bhupen, our youngest team lead, has high standards and works harder than anyone. This week he snapped at the intern, Sahil, over a late file: "Is this how you were raised?" Afterwards he came to me looking shaken. He said, "That's exactly what my father used to say to me." We talked it through. He said he wants to keep his father's discipline and care for detail, but not the sharpness. He apologised to Sahil in person today and has asked me to tell him if I hear that tone again. I will check in with both of them next week.

qa.q: What did Bhupen say to Sahil?
qa.a: "Is this how you were raised?"

qa.q: How did Bhupen feel after snapping at Sahil?
qa.a: Shaken, recognising his father's exact words coming out of his own mouth.

qa.q: What choices did Bhupen make?
qa.a: To keep his father's discipline and care for detail but drop the sharpness, to apologise to Sahil, and to ask the supervisor to flag the tone.

qa.q: How might Sahil have felt hearing the remark?
qa.a: Hurt and humiliated over a late file.

grounding: An adult notices he sounds like his strict father and chooses to keep the diligence but drop the sharpness.

subtype: Choosing which parental traits to keep [Response]
passage:
Sunday.
Yash asked me to check his job application today, and I heard myself say, "Did you even read it before sending it to me? Sloppy." Word for word, Papa's voice. I saw Yash's shoulders drop, the way mine used to. It shook me. Tonight I made two lists. From Papa, keep: showing up early, finishing what you start, checking every detail. From Papa, drop: the sneer, the word "sloppy", making people feel small. I called Yash, apologised, and went through his application properly, line by line. He was quiet at first, then laughed at my notes. I'm keeping the details. I'm leaving the sneer with Papa.
Anand

qa.q: What word did Anand use about Yash's application?
qa.a: "Sloppy."

qa.q: How did Anand feel after hearing Papa's voice in those words?
qa.a: Shaken, seeing Yash's shoulders drop the way Anand's used to.

qa.q: What did Anand decide to keep and drop?
qa.a: Keep showing up early, finishing what you start and checking every detail; drop the sneer and making people feel small.

qa.q: How did Yash react to the apology and the careful check?
qa.a: He was quiet at first, then laughed at the notes, probably relieved.

grounding: An adult hears a strict father's sharpness in their own words and chooses to keep his diligence but drop the sneer.

subtype: Choosing which parental traits to keep [Response]
passage:

passage:
"Here. For you." Saurabh slid a shiny tiger sticker across the desk.
Kavitha looked at it, then at him. "Why?"
"No reason. It's winter. Stickers are... nice in winter."
"Yesterday you called me 'slowpoke' in front of everyone."
Saurabh studied his pencil. "The sticker's really good, though."
"It is good." She didn't pick it up.
"Okay." He took a breath. "I'm sorry I called you slowpoke. It was mean. You're not slow."
Kavitha smiled a little and stuck the tiger on her notebook.
"Thanks for saying sorry," she said. "The sticker was nice. The sorry was better."

qa.q: What sticker did Saurabh give Kavitha?
qa.a: A shiny tiger sticker.

qa.q: Why did Saurabh give the sticker without saying why?
qa.a: He felt guilty about calling her slowpoke and hoped the gift would cancel it without having to say the uncomfortable words.

qa.q: What finished the repair?
qa.a: A real apology: "I'm sorry I called you slowpoke. It was mean."

qa.q: How did Kavitha feel about the sticker on its own?
qa.a: Unsure and still hurt; she didn't pick it up until he apologised.

grounding: A child who called a friend a name brings a sticker without mentioning it, and an apology finishes the repair.

passage: Last Christmas I called my friend Anirban "crybaby" when he cried during the football match. The next day I felt bad, so I brought him my best marble, the blue one, and put it on his desk without saying anything. He took it, but he didn't smile. At lunch he sat with someone else. I didn't understand. I had given him my best marble! My mother said, "A marble is nice. But did you tell him you were sorry for the word?" I hadn't. The next morning I said it: "Sorry I called you crybaby." Anirban shrugged and said, "Okay." Then he let me sit with him again. I'm Divyansh. Now I know the words matter more than the marble.

qa.q: What did Divyansh bring Anirban?
qa.a: The best marble, the blue one.

qa.q: Why didn't Divyansh understand Anirban's reaction?
qa.a: Divyansh felt confused and hurt, thinking the best marble should fix things, without realising the word needed an apology.

qa.q: What did Divyansh do next?
qa.a: Said sorry for the word "crybaby" the next morning, which let them sit together again.

qa.q: How might Anirban have felt getting the marble without an apology?
qa.a: Still hurt, since the name-calling hadn't been acknowledged.

grounding: A child brings a friend a gift after calling him a name, and learns that an apology is what finishes the repair.

passage: Camp counsellor's note, summer camp, day four. Yesterday Anirban called Asif "stinky" after football, and a few boys laughed. Today, without a word, Anirban left his new rocket pencil on Asif's bunk. Asif looked confused, then pushed it back. I spoke to Anirban quietly. He said, "I gave him the rocket pencil. That's sorry." I told him the pencil was a kind thought, but Asif still needed to hear the words. After lunch, Anirban said, "Sorry I called you stinky." Asif nodded and took the pencil. At pickup I will tell both families how the two boys sorted it out.

qa.q: What was on Anirban's new pencil?
qa.a: A rocket.

qa.q: Why did Anirban think the pencil was enough?
qa.a: He felt guilty and thought the gift said sorry for him, avoiding the harder words.

qa.q: What did the counsellor explain?
qa.a: That the pencil was a kind thought, but Asif still needed to hear the words.

qa.q: Why might Asif have pushed the pencil back?
qa.a: He was still hurt and confused; a gift without an apology didn't undo being called stinky.

grounding: A child who called another boy a name leaves him a gift, and a counsellor helps him add the actual apology.

passage: After shouting "You never listen to me!" at her mum about the school trip, Freya slammed her bedroom door so hard the pictures shook. An hour later, her brother Emeka came home to find their flat in Leeds spotless. Freya had vacuumed, washed every dish, and folded laundry nobody had asked her to fold. She was now making her mum's favourite tea, with the good biscuits on a plate. She set it beside her mum's laptop and walked away without a word. Emeka raised an eyebrow. Their mum looked at the tea, then at the closed door. "That's lovely," she said quietly to Emeka. "But I'd rather she just talked to me." Later, Freya came out and said it: "Sorry I shouted."

qa.q: What did Freya shout at her mum?
qa.a: "You never listen to me!"

qa.q: Why did Freya clean the whole flat and make tea?
qa.a: She felt guilty about shouting, and the generous actions were a way to show it without saying sorry.

qa.q: What did Freya's mum need beyond the tea?
qa.a: To hear Freya talk to her, which came when Freya finally said, "Sorry I shouted."

qa.q: How did Mum feel about the tea?
qa.a: Touched but still wanting words, saying she'd rather Freya just talked to her.

grounding: A teenager who yelled at a parent cleans the whole flat and makes tea without a word, and the parent still needs a spoken sorry.

passage: At the parent-teacher meeting in the school hall, Tanvir's mother, Ayesha, mentioned his low physics mark to the teacher, and Tanvir snapped, loudly, "Can you stop embarrassing me?" A few parents turned. His mother went quiet. For the rest of the evening, Tanvir was the perfect son. He carried her bag, fetched her a cup of chai from the canteen, held the door, even thanked the physics teacher. His mother accepted everything with a small nod. In the auto home, she finally said, "The chai was sweet. But you shouted at me in front of people." Tanvir looked out of the window for a long time. Then: "I'm sorry, Ammi. I was embarrassed. It wasn't your fault." She squeezed his hand.

passage: Exam week, three papers in four days, and Uma had no energy for drama. On Tuesday, as she rushed to the exam hall, Naveen caught her with a gift bag: expensive wireless earphones, still boxed. He smiled broadly. "For my favourite person!" Uma felt a strange heaviness. It was as if Sunday had been wiped off the board without either of them saying a word. She took a breath. "That's generous, Naveen. But I'd rather we talked about Sunday. What you said hurt." passage: Two days after Rafiq mocked Neelam's accent in the Delhi college canteen, doing a loud impression while everyone laughed, he turned up at her hostel gate with a box of expensive chocolates and a huge smile. "Peace offering!" he said. Neelam held the box. It was beautiful. And somehow she felt worse, as if the chocolates were meant to make the canteen disappear. She thought about just saying thanks and moving on. Instead she said, "Thank you, Rafiq. But honestly, I'd rather hear you say sorry. The impression really hurt." Rafiq's smile dropped. He looked at his shoes. "Yeah. It was a stupid thing to do. I'm sorry." Neelam nodded. "Now we can share the chocolates."

qa.q: What did Rafiq bring to the hostel gate?
qa.a: A box of expensive chocolates.

qa.q: Why did the chocolates make Neelam feel worse?

qa.a: She thanked him but said she'd rather hear sorry because the impression hurt, which led to a real apology.

qa.q: How did Rafiq react to Neelam's honesty?
qa.a: His smile dropped, he looked at his shoes, and he apologised.

grounding: A student mocked by a friend receives chocolates instead of an apology and kindly asks for words instead.

passage:
"Ganga! I got you this." Himani held out a silk scarf, the expensive kind from the market.
"Oh. It's beautiful. What's the occasion?"
"No occasion. Just because."
Ganga turned the scarf over. "Is this about Friday?"
Himani's smile stayed on. "Friday? What about Friday?"
"When you told the group my painting looked like a child's."
"Oh, that. I was joking."
"It didn't feel like a joke."
"Well, that's why I got the scarf!"
Ganga folded it gently. "It's lovely, Himani. But I'd rather we talk. A gift feels like wiping it away."
Himani's smile faded. She sat down. "Okay. I'm sorry. That was unkind."

qa.q: What did Himani say about Ganga's painting?
qa.a: That it looked like a child's.

qa.q: How does Ganga feel about the scarf?
qa.a: Uneasy and still hurt, as if the gift is wiping away the insult without any talk.

qa.q: What did Ganga do that worked?
qa.a: Named Friday, said it didn't feel like a joke, and kindly said she'd rather talk than take a gift in its place.

qa.q: How does Himani respond when Ganga says she'd rather talk?
qa.a: Her smile fades; she sits down and apologises properly.

grounding: A person insulted by a friend is given an expensive scarf instead of an apology and kindly says talking matters more.

subtype: Overworking to make up for a mistake [Actor]
passage:
Thursday, 11:40 p.m.
Still at the office. Third week of late nights since I missed the client deadline. Yash offered again today to take the testing off my plate. I said no, again. I think I believe that if I suffer enough, the mistake will be cancelled. But nobody asked me to suffer. The manager has already moved on; the client got the work two days late and was fine. I'm the only one still punishing me. My eyes burn, and I snapped at my sister on the phone. Tomorrow I'm going to do what I've avoided: tell the manager plainly, "I missed it, here's what I'll do differently," and let Yash help. And go home by seven.
Hemant

qa.q: How might Yash feel being turned down again?
qa.a: Puzzled and a bit shut out, wanting to help a tired colleague.

grounding: An employee who missed a deadline overworks for weeks and refuses help as penance, then decides simple ownership costs less.

passage: Devika had been the new block agriculture officer for six months when she forgot to file the seed order on time, and the paddy seed reached the village a week late. The farmers grumbled but managed. Devika did not. For a month she rode her scooter to the fields at dawn, stayed at the office till nine, and refused when her colleague Parveen offered to share the field visits. "I made the mess," she said. Her mother noticed she had stopped eating properly. One evening Parveen sat on the edge of her desk. "You've paid ten times over. Nobody's asking for more. Just tell the committee what happened and how you'll track orders now." Devika's eyes stung. The next day she did, in five sentences. The committee nodded and moved on.
